en: Now begins the fourth chapter:
That supreme Brahman, by the knowledge of which liberation is attained while living—liberation devoid of departure from the body or transition to another state—that am I, Rāma, the fearless one. (1)
START BsRp_4,1.1.1:
Repetition [is required] because of the instruction being given more than once. Oṃ!
Repetition [is required] because of the instruction being given more than once.
Having examined the means (*sādhana*), the result (*phala*) is now examined; thus, he states the connection between the chapters as being that of cause and effect with the words "In the third.
He says "by way of occasion" (*prasaṅgena*) because, following the discussion of the result, the departure [of the soul] and the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) are investigated.
Previously, the means such as renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) were considered directly as they were stated in the Śruti.

Now, repetition (*āvṛtti*) and other matters, which are to be understood through the presumption of the result (*phalārthāpatti*), are considered prior to the section on "immediate connection" (*adyāśleṣādhikara�ṇa*).

Starting from that point, the first quarter (*pāda*) deals with liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); the second quarter with the departure of the soul (*utkrānti*); the third with the determination of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) and the destination; and the fourth with the determination of the fruits of knowledge and meditation (*upāsana*). This is the analysis of the subject matter of the quarters.

Having restated the subject of the first section—the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*)—he states the doubt arising from the observation of two modes of practice: "Or rather, the Self... (*ātmā vā iti*).

Since all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) consist of an inquiry into the means and fruits of the knowledge of the Self as revealed in the Vedas (*śruti*), the connections between the scriptures, the chapters, and the sections have been stated. The connection between the individual sections (*pādas*) arises from their relation to their respective subject matters (*padārtha*).

Regarding the doubt that there is no specific distinction in the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of hearing and so forth—just as there is no specific distinction in liberation—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated by way of an intermediate connection characterized by an analogy: "What, then, [is the case]? and so on.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since hearing and so forth have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) like the *prayāja* offerings, their performance should be done only once; however, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) like the act of threshing (*avaghāta*), there must be repetition as long as the result persists. One might object: "But surely, the intention of the scripture is that the means must be repeated, because it would otherwise be impossible to justify the instruction that it is not to be done only once. This is the doubt raised by the phrase "nanu asakṛt" ("But [it says] 'not once'").

He says, "Even so," [meaning] that since it has been stated more than once that hearing and the other [means] are for the purpose of establishing their combination (*samuccaya*), there is no intention regarding repetition (*āvṛtti*) because it can be explained otherwise.
He also states that there is no repetition even in the means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Saguna [Brahman]: "once.
Although the repeated instruction is established otherwise as indicating either repetition or combination, [it does not necessarily imply both].

Nevertheless, since it is illogical to postulate a mere unseen result when a seen one is possible—and because repetition by way of repeated hearing and so forth has been observed to have direct realization as its fruit in the case of [identifying] musical notes like *ṣaḍja*—the statement "repeatedly" indicates repetition, being favored by the maxim that "what has a seen purpose [does not require an unseen one]. Thus he says:
"Because it culminates in realization."
But as for meditation (*dhyāna*), because the word "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) is heard in the scripture, it does not have a purely objective meaning; thus he says, "Moreover" (*apica*).

Although the word "meditation" (*upāsti*) has the sense of repetition, how is repetition established in the case of the ego-apprehensions (*ahaṅgraha*) denoted by the word "knowing" (*veda*)? To this he says: "Of *vid* and *upāsti*.
He provides an example of the two words having the same meaning: "In some places... (*kvacid*).

When it was said that whatever Raikva knows— that reality of the vital breath (*prāṇa-tattva*)— and that everything else known by anyone other than Raikva is included within its fruit, another swan said to the swan, "In this way, I have described that Raikva as being preeminent. Having heard this, Jānaśruti went to Raikva and spoke.
"O Blessed One, instruct me— that is, teach me— this deity known to Raikva. Thus,

the repetition of meditation, which is the means for the direct realization of both the qualified (saguṇa) and unqualified (nirguṇa) [Brahman], is both scripturally enjoined and established by the very nature of the case, because it has a visible purpose.
However, as for hearing and reflection, since the instruction is given repeatedly, repetition is established by the very nature of the matter; this is the distinction. //1//
And because of the indicative mark. (BBs 4.1.2)
Because one performs meditation by identifying the single Āditya with the *udgītha*, Kauṣītaki said to his son, "You are my only son";
therefore, you should not act in that way, but rather "turn toward many rays and Āditya"—that is, turn toward them individually. The elision of the *t* (in *paryāvartayatāt*) is a Vedic archaism.

Here, by the word "paryāvṛtti" (repetition), the repetition of the meditation on the *udgītha* is stated as an established fact; then, because of the common characteristic of being a form of meditation (*dhyānatva*), or because of the common characteristic of culminating in a fruit (*phalaparyantatva*), he states that repetition is established for hearing, reflection, and meditation everywhere through this indicative mark (*liṅga*), saying: "And from the indicative mark.

Thus, repetition has been stated regarding the means for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of both the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*). In that context, having accepted the repetition of the meditation on the qualified and so forth, he raises an objection regarding the repetition of hearing the unqualified and so forth, starting with the words "Here [the opponent] says," etc., [asking]:
Is [the scripture] capable of producing the direct realization of the unqualified, or not?
Having stated that repetition is useless because direct realization is accomplished from a statement heard even once in the first case, he raises the second objection with the word "once" (*sakṛt*).
He says "no" (*na*) to the point that for one who is incapable, the result does not arise even through repetition.
The phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means: even if there is capability through the accompaniment of reasoning in one who is inherently incapable.

He raises an objection, saying "But it might be so," [meaning] that even when indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) has arisen through both verbal testimony and reasoning, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is required for the sake of direct realization (*aparokṣajñāna*).

He refutes this, saying "Not even by repetition," because those two [means] have the inherent nature of being causes for indirect knowledge; therefore, even with repetition, there would be no direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*).
He states "Therefore," meaning that whether those two possess the capacity for direct intuition or the capacity for indirect knowledge, in either case, they do not depend upon repetition.
He says "nor" (*na ca*) because there is no fixed rule regarding repetition even due to the diversity of knowers (*pramātṛ*).
He says "moreover" (*api ca*) because it is likewise so due to the partlessness (*anaṃśatva*) of the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

For there would be two kinds of qualified persons (*adhikārī*): one whose obstacles such as all forms of doubt (*asaṃbhāvanā*) and the like have been removed through practice in previous births, and another who still possesses such obstacles.

Regarding this, he provides the resolution: "To this it is said. He states that the first [repetition] is accepted as being purposeless, whereas for the second, there is a dependence on it for the sake of removing obstacles;
thus he says, "For instance," providing the evidence (*liṅga*) for the fact that repetition serves to remove obstacles.

Just as the auditory organ, though capable of directly perceiving the distinctions between musical notes such as *ṣaḍja* and others, requires repeated practice, so too the sentence—though capable of bringing about the direct realization of Brahman as the Self—requires that [practice]. Relying on this experience, he says: "For there is nothing impossible in what is perceived. Since the referent indicated by the words *tat* and *tvam* is difficult to comprehend, there is the possibility of obstacles such as doubt induced by ignorance; therefore, repetition must be accepted for the destruction of those obstacles. With this in mind, preceded by a distinction between the expressed and the indicated meanings, he says "Moreover," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that repetition is useless because the object of knowledge is partless, he says: "Even though... The meaning is that the practice of [meditating] "I am not the body, I am not the senses" is appropriate for the purpose of dispelling superimposed parts.

If the meaning of the sentence has already been known, how can there be a rule for practice? For it is impossible to practice a cognition that is already valid knowledge, and it is likewise impossible for one who already possesses knowledge to be subject to rules such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth. To this he says: "tat tu" (but that). The meaning is that the restriction of the activities of hearing and so forth is performed precisely prior to the arising of knowledge.
He restates what was said regarding the excessive doubt with the words "of those who...
He expresses the excessive doubt with the words "it is true...
The meaning is that, because it contradicts the direct perception of being a sufferer, the cognition of oneness does not arise from the statement.
He states "no" and so forth to show that there is no contradiction because perception is erroneous.
The meaning is: suffering and the rest are not attributes of the self because they are visible, like the body and so forth;
nor are they the very nature of the self because, even when the self exists, they do not persist, as in the case of consciousness by way of contrast.

He says "Therefore" to show that the experience of the meaning of the sentence is not contradicted, because cognitions of suffering and so forth regarding the Self, which is consciousness and free from suffering, are merely errors. To the question, "Even when such experience has arisen, why should one not continue to perform practices such as repetition [of the mantra]? he says "And not thus.

There is a distinction: *rati* is desire; satisfaction through the desire for the Self is the cessation of thirst for sense objects, and through that, contentment is the experience of the bliss of the Self.

[Objection: Surely, in the case of repetition, activity must be said to proceed from an injunction (*niyoga*); and if that were so, because of the cognition of being enjoined, there could be no realization of the self as a non-agent. To this, he says: "In that case too" (*tatrāpi*). The meaning is that even when repetition is accepted, neither the teacher nor anyone else would cause one to engage [in practice] by means of an injunction—by displacing the experience "I am a non-agent"—because of the aforementioned defect. If so, how then does engagement occur? To this, he says: "But he who... (*yas tu*).
The meaning is: "due to a lack of eloquence," that is, because of a lack of confidence and so forth.

The meaning is that one should engage in repetition and other such methods for the sake of establishing the primary goal, using words such as "it must be recited" in accordance with the student's intellect. //2//
"But they acknowledge [the self] as 'the Self' and cause others to grasp it as such. (BS 4.1.3)
However, people accept [the self] as "I" and grasp it as such.

Since the repetition of meditation and so forth was mentioned previously, depending on that, he states a doubt regarding the time of repeating meditation for the sake of the knowledge of reality: "Is one to meditate 'I am Brahman,' or 'The Lord is my master'?"—thus expressing the doubt through the measures of identity and difference. This is what the word "yaḥ" (who/that) refers to.

In the passage beginning with "He is known from the word alone," [the author] raises a doubt by questioning how there can be a determination of identity through scriptural texts on non-difference such as "This Self is Brahman.

He states that the doubt arises because one relies on the superiority of perception and other means of knowledge regarding difference, supported by scriptural texts on difference—this is what is meant by "It is said.
Regarding both the secondary and primary senses of the non-difference scriptures, there is a result in each case.

Although this resolution of contradictions with perception and other means of knowledge is properly situated in the second chapter, it is connected here because the certainty that the scriptural texts on unity are not contradictory is an internal factor for meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He states, "Not I," [implying] that the perception of identity between two contradictory things is unestablished.

Furthermore, having raised the alternatives—whether unity consists in the Lord being merely the individual soul (*jīva*), or the individual soul being merely the Lord—he refutes them in turn, beginning with "And of the Lord... and so forth.

He raises the objection that meditation on unity must be practiced for the sake of validating the scriptural teaching of oneness, stating: "Even though there is difference. He replies: "Granted," meaning that while meditation on unity is indeed what we ourselves accept, actual oneness does not exist.

Since it is impossible for the non-difference scriptures to be secondary (gauṇa) when they have as their purport the unprecedented (apūrva) fruit-bearing [knowledge], and since the difference scriptures merely restate an imagined difference, and since even perception and other means of knowledge have that [imagined difference] as their object, and since contradictory attributes—like those of a reflection and its original—are unreal, primary unity is established; this is demonstrated by the words beginning with "evam" (thus).
It is not the Lord's state of being a living soul (jīvatva) that is to be established, such that the Lord would cease to exist; rather, it is the living soul's state of being the Lord (īśvaratva).

Nor is there an absence of qualified candidates [for this teaching] in this way, because we accept a distinction among qualified candidates prior to the awakening to oneness; thus he says, "As for what was said," and so forth.
One who has faith in the truth of the Veda raises an objection: "Because of the absence of perception and the other means of knowledge."

Since sequence and accent do not exist in the phonemes themselves, their superimposition must be said to reside in the perceived sounds; and thus, the falsity of the Veda—which consists of phonemes qualified by superimposed sequence and accent—is unavoidable.
The disputants' adherence to its truthfulness is merely a manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, he says "No," [meaning] that the absence of the Veda's truthfulness is not a fault.
He challenges this ignorance with the question: "Of what? (kasya).

He says, "You who... because, since the question and so forth are rooted in ignorance, it is illogical for you to raise such an objection; the sense is that [the objection] arises from the premise that the question is based on ignorance.
He raises an objection, saying "But surely...", wondering how there could be ignorance in me, who am non-different from the Omniscient One.

Prior to the knowledge of non-difference, you yourself, as pure consciousness (cinmātra), are the locus of ignorance, because it is impossible to deny ignorance that is established by experience. However, upon the arising of knowledge, since that indeterminable [ignorance] is sublated, there is no requirement for a locus; thus he says, "If this is so. He further states, "And that which... to show that other defects are also refuted by its indeterminability. //3//
Not in the symbols, for he is not that. (BBs 4.1.4)
"Not in the symbol, for he [the Self] is not there.
Since meditation is possible in both ways, a doubt arises:

just as "seizing by the I" (*ahaṅgraha*) was prescribed regarding Brahman because of the existence of non-difference, so too, since symbols are modifications of Brahman, they are non-different from Brahman which is non-different from the individual soul; thus, because non-difference from the individual soul exists, "seizing by the I" should be performed even with respect to the symbols.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based on the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In this regard, there is no distinction between meditations on symbols (*pratīkopāsti*) and meditations involving the grasping of the self (*ahaṅgrahopāsti*).
However, the result in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the establishment of a distinction.

The connection of these three sections (*adhikaraṇa*) with the current chapter (*pāda*) is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*), because they have arisen in the context of the meditation on the identity of Brahman; this is the distinction.

Is the identification with the "I" (*ahaṅgraha*) in the case of symbols (*pratīka*) due to the force of experiencing them as the Self, or because there exists an actual non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and [Brahman]?
Regarding the first [point], he says "not today," meaning "for he does not experience [it].
Regarding the second, he refutes it by showing its lack of proof, saying "as for that which..."

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible for a modification (*vikāra*) to be identical in essence with Brahman, their identity must be stated as one resulting from sublation (*bādha*); however, if the symbol (*pratīka*) were thus sublated, the injunction for meditation upon it would cease to exist.
Furthermore, the operation of the injunction for meditation must be stated to occur without the sublation of agency and so forth, because such an injunction is untenable if there is sublation.

Consequently, it is not logical to postulate a meditation involving the identification of the self (*ahaṅgraha-upāsti*) with symbols by means of the knowledge of identity with Brahman—which is rooted in sublation—as an intermediary step.
He states that [the view] is contradicted by sublation: "And not of Brahman.

Therefore, since there is a difference in essential nature between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the symbol (*pratīka*), and because no injunction for the practice of identification (*ahaṅgraha*) is heard in this context, he states the resulting conclusion: "And therefore...

Just as there is no mutual identity between a gold necklace and a golden swastika despite their unity in the form of gold, so too there is an equal distinction between the individual soul and the symbol despite their unity in the form of Brahman.

And if, because of the certainty that those two do not exist apart from the substratum (dharmin), there were an identity of substance (vastvaikya), then it would follow that the practice of meditation (upāsanā) is abolished; this is the meaning [of verse 4].
The vision of Brahman [should be applied] to the sacrificial post because of its excellence. (BBs 4.1.5)
The view of Brahman [is mentioned] because of its superiority.
"Connection" consists in having the same object.
He states the seed of doubt by means of a question, beginning with "Why? and so forth.

The grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) that is heard in the text is not primary, because a non-difference between Brahman and its modification is impossible, like that between a cow and a horse;
nor is it based on the relationship of material cause and effect (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva).
Because the sentence would result in having Brahman as its primary purport by way of modifying or subverting [the literal sense], this is not an acceptable consequence;
for it would contradict the injunctive scriptural text: "One should meditate on Name as Brahman."
Furthermore, because it would follow that the mention of specific names would be purposeless;
for if the intent were Brahman, one would have to say "everything is Brahman.

Therefore, by process of elimination, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) alone is the cause of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and since there is no restrictive factor regarding superimposition, there is doubt—this is the meaning.

"The principle that 'even the inferior among the superior and the inferior is to be worshipped because it yields fruit' serves as the regulator"—this is stated with a sense of dissatisfaction, hence he says "Or rather" (*athavā*).
Here, the result is the accomplishment of the worship of Brahman through the perception of it as a modification (*vikāra*);

however, in the final view (*siddhānta*), since the worship of Brahman by means of the perception of it as a modification would lead to its degradation and thus fail to establish the attainment of fruit, the result is that the modifications themselves are to be worshipped through the perception of them as the superior Brahman.
Furthermore, when a meaning that is not contradicted by worldly logic is possible, a contradictory meaning should not be accepted, as it would entail the consequence of sin (pratyavāya).
Moreover, since there is no prior contradiction, it is logical to accept the primary sense for the words "Āditya" and so forth when they are first heard,
while the word "Brahman" is understood through the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of a meditative vision (dṛṣṭi).
And thus, he states that the meaning of the sentence is precisely that the sun and so forth are to be meditated upon through the vision of Brahman—by saying, "and because of being first.
He provides another reason for the word *brahman* itself having the sense of "vision" by saying, "because it ends with the particle *iti*.
The meaning is that it is well known in common usage that a word preceded by the particle *iti* indicates the action with which it is syntactically connected.
He states that, because of the mention of "the second," only the sun and so forth constitute the objects of meditation—this being expressed by the words "The remainder of the passage also.
He restates the principle already mentioned—that only the superior [deity] is to be meditated upon—with the words "As for what was said.
He then states that this established principle is sublated by the two mentions of "the second" and by common worldly reasoning, with the words "That..."
If Brahman is not the object of worship, how can it be the bestower of the fruit?
To this he says: "But the fruit...

Furthermore, even though Brahman is a qualifier of that modification which attains excellence through a particular vision, its status as the object of worship does not cease; to this he says: "And such... (verse 5).
And the conceptions of the Ādityas and others [are to be applied] to the subsidiary members [of the sacrifice], because it is appropriate.
Beginning with the Ādityas: in the worlds known as Earth, Fire, Atmosphere, Sun, and Heaven, the Sāman is fivefold through its parts— the *hiṅkāra*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratīhāra*, and *nidhana*.
The distinction is that [the Sāman] is called *ādi* by those who have two additional *bhaktis*, and *upadrava* by those who have seven parts (*saptāṃśa*).
Therefore, because of this lack of specific knowledge, there is doubt.
He states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of a counter-example, saying "In that case," based on the lack of certainty regarding superiority as in the previous instance.

He states the primary prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by means of an illustration: "Or rather," [meaning] that because the Udgītha and other ritual forms are superior due to their proximity to the fruit—unlike the perfected forms such as Āditya and so on—there is a restrictive rule regarding their being qualifiers, just like Brahman.
One should understand that the very establishment of each respective position constitutes the result of the preceding and succeeding arguments.

Furthermore, regarding the point that the perception of the limbs (aṅga) occurs only in those things which are not actually limbs, he states the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting in the use of words denoting "limbs" with respect to them: "And thus, this very... and so forth.
This means that this Sāman called "Agni" is *adhyūḍha*—that is, situated above—this Ṛc which has the form of the earth.
Just as the Sāman is perceived upon the Ṛc, Agni is perceived upon the earth;
therefore, because of this similarity, meditation is enjoined such that the earth itself is the Ṛc and Agni is the Sāman.

In this regard, if there were a perception of the earth and fire as being the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*—which are auxiliary elements of the ritual—then the application of the terms *Ṛk* and *Sāman* to the earth and fire would not be possible; regarding this, he provides an example with the words "as [the term] *kṣattṛ*.
Therefore, the meaning is that because the usage [of the terms] cannot otherwise be accounted for, there is a perception of the earth and fire as the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*.
And he says "moreover" (api ca) to show that it is exactly so by means of the locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*).
[The text mentions] the *sāman* known as *gāyatra*.
Furthermore, he says "firstly" (*prathama*) to show that it is also so by way of the logic of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the preceding section.
He establishes the conclusion that the limbs [of the sacrifice] are to be meditated upon with the thought that they are the Bodiless One (Anaṅga), saying "Thus.
For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of these meditations is the success of the ritual action, and that is possible when the limbs are being refined by those meditations.
The meaning is that the limbs produce the *apūrva* (unseen potency) of the primary rite, which is conducive to their own perfection.

Now, one might object: where the fruit of meditations (*upāsanā*) is heard as being dependent on the limbs of the primary rite through the mediation of the *apūrva*, let there be the status of those limbs as objects of meditation (*upāsya*) for the sake of the attainment of that fruit; but how can there be such a distinction of objects of meditation in those meditations whose fruits—such as the worlds and so forth—are independent of that [primary rite]?
Thus he raises the objection: "Let it be so.

Just as the *godohana* vessel, although its fruit is independent, is accepted as having a fruit only by way of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to another rite, so too in the case of meditations (*upāsanā*) whose fruits are the worlds and so forth, the postulation of a fruit occurs only by way of the auxiliary nature of the ritual apūrva; for only one who is already qualified for the ritual is eligible for meditations based on those auxiliaries.
Therefore, he provides the resolution that the limbs themselves are what are to be meditated upon with the words "even in those.
He rejects the previously stated position—that there is no fixed rule because no superiority can be determined—by saying "the essence of the fruit.
Furthermore, he states that the limb is to be meditated upon on the strength of the opening statement (upakrama) with the words "moreover" (api ca).
The meaning is that there is an addition [to the list] of qualities such as being the most flavorful (*rasatamatva*).
He refutes the second prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "As for what was said," and so forth.
"Attaining the state of action" (*karmabhūyam*) means attaining the nature of action (*karmātmakatvam*).

Since it might be argued that if the ritual acts are viewed as having the nature of the perfected Sun and so forth, their status as ritual acts would be lost, he says: "by way of the state of being the Sun and so forth. Just as the perception of fire in a boy is figurative, the cognitions of the Sun and so forth regarding the *udgītha* and other parts of the sacrifice are merely secondary; therefore, they do not sublate the status of those acts as rituals. The intention is that the cognition of non-membership with respect to the members [of the sacrifice] is not contradictory.
He refutes the previously stated impossibility of practical application with the words: "this very [point]."
He states the relationship that serves as the seed for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) with the words "and *lakṣaṇā*.
In the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," *lakṣaṇā* is observed to function through a direct relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with the bank;
in "the boy is fire," *lakṣaṇā* is observed to function through an indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) consisting of the possession of qualities such as purity residing in fire.

And thus, even in this case where the view of Earth and Fire is superimposed upon the *Ṛk* and *Sāman*, it is logical that the words *Ṛk* and *Sāman* indicate Earth and Fire through a mediate relationship known as "being the object of vision" with respect to their own primary denotations; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Is it not improper for a word expressing a mere symbol (*pratīka*) to have an indicative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the object of meditation? For instance, the word 'charioteer' (*kṣattṛ*) is used [metaphorically] for a king. To this, he raises the doubt: "In that regard, although... and so forth.

Nevertheless, because of the connection between the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, it was stated separately regarding the primary pair—earth and fire—that "the *sāman* is mounted upon this *ṛc*"; thus, if earth and fire were understood here in the phrase "upon this" (*etasyām*) as well, there would be a redundancy.

Therefore, the meaning is that the terms for the symbols (*pratīka*) are applied to earth and fire specifically because of their proximity as symbols, and by means of the perception of non-difference from the symbols, for the sake of strengthening that [perceived] identity.
If it is then asked, "In that case, the word *kṣattṛ* (charioteer) would also apply to the king," he says: "The *kṣattri*... [and so on].
The meaning is that some cause for the application [of a term] must be stated, but it is not the case that the application is to be established merely because a cause exists.

"Kṣattṛ" means a charioteer; when he performs the duties of that office, such as driving the chariot, like a king, then the word *kṣattṛ* also applies to the king—this is the literal meaning of the words.

He states another reason for the view that the earth and so forth are to be meditated upon as the *Ṛk* and so forth, beginning with the words "This [world]," etc. He rejects the notion that the worlds are the objects of meditation by means of the locative case in the phrase "likewise in the worlds" (*tathā lokeṣu*).

The meaning is: rather than you having to violate both the accusative and the locative cases—by interpreting the instruction "one should meditate on the worlds as the *Sāman*" as "one should meditate on the *Sāman* as the worlds"—it is better to violate the locative alone, by interpreting it as "one should meditate on the *Sāman* as the worlds."

The meaning is that by this—namely, by the parsimony of breaking down the case-ending into a single one—it has been explained that the *Gāyatra* Sāman is to be meditated upon as having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its self.
[Objection: But how is a decision reached when there is equality of case-endings? To this he says: "Even where...

Even for one who has departed by any particular path, if the attainment of the world of Brahman were possible, then the injunction to remember the path as a supplement to the meditation (*vidyā*) would result in having only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, [the attainment occurs] only by means of the path remembered daily.
The sense is that going [there] is logical.
"Hārda" means the Brahman within the heart.
"Viṣvaṅ" means other various kinds of channels belonging to others; such is the meaning.

The channel named Suṣumnā, having issued from the heart, reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) by way of the right eye, the palate, the throat, the interior of the chest, and the middle of the nasal septum; it is unified with the rays of the sun and constitutes the path to the world of Brahmā for the practitioner—this is established. //17//
He follows the rays. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.18)
"Following the rays" (*raśmyanusārī*).
Having first clarified the context, he states the subject of the disciple's following the rays with the words beginning "it exists" (*asti*), etc.
The meaning is that when this departure occurs at the end of the *prārabdha* (projected karma), then one departs by means of these very rays connected to the channels (*nāḍī*).
Regarding this, since no specific time for the connection [of the rays] is heard mentioned, and because the rays are absent at night, he states a doubt: "Now, what...
The connection [of the discussion] is due to the fact that the rays connected with the channels (nāḍīs) mentioned previously are what must be relied upon here.
In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), there is a waiting for sunrise by one who has died at night, for the sake of reaching the rays.
Thinking that [the objection] does not exist in the established doctrine (siddhānta), he asserts the established doctrine with the words: "without distinction" (aviśeṣeṇa). //18//

If it be argued that [the soul] does not exist at night, we say no; for the connection [of the soul with its faculties] persists as long as the body exists, and scripture also demonstrates this. (BS 4.2.19)
Having set forth the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with the words beginning with "niśi" (at night).
The channels (*śirā*) extend—that is, they become expanded—and are "sṛpta," meaning interconnected.
He provides the reasoning for the existence of the connection mentioned in the scripture at night with the word "nidāgha" (in the heat of summer).
In that case, one might object that heat would be perceived during the nights of winter and so forth; to this he says, "slight" (*stoka*).
The statement that the sun bestows day even at night is intended to mean only the persistence of a few rays.

Furthermore, if the upward journey of one who dies at night were to occur without connection to the rays, then the scriptural mention of the rays would have to be restricted to those who die during the day; and if there were no upward journey, there would be no engagement with the knowledge (*vidyā*) [of the path].
It might be argued that there is no waiting for the upward journey; but this cannot be maintained,

because if the body were consumed by fire before the emergence of the rays, it would follow that waiting for the sun is useless, and furthermore, it would contradict the scriptural texts concerning the absence of waiting.
Therefore, whenever one has died, through the attainment of the rays, there is an immediate arrival at the world of Brahman. //19//
And for this reason, [the same applies] even during the southern course of the sun. (BsRp_4,2.10.20)

Thus, regarding the doubt as to whether a wise person who dies during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) attains the fruit of knowledge or not—given that the scripture declares the fruit of knowledge as if it were constant and that there are scriptural texts praising the northern course (uttarāyaṇa)—the author extends the previously stated reasons to this case: "And therefore, even in the southern course. Having raised the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), he dispels it with the words beginning "The northern course," and so forth.

If the death of the ignorant occurs during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) by chance, it is praiseworthy; Bhīṣma’s waiting was for the purpose of maintaining the established custom consisting of the declarations of those who possess higher knowledge.
As for the scriptural statement regarding "six months," it will be explained that it refers to the deity presiding over the northern course.
Thus, since the deity is eternally present, there is no contradiction in attaining that [state] through knowledge even during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). This is the intended meaning. //20//
And these two are recorded in the Smṛti with respect to yogins; moreover, these two belong to the Smṛti tradition.

He raises an objection regarding the predominance of time by saying, "But if... [nanu ceti]. He states that there is no contradiction by saying, "The yogins...": while we have stated that for one who meditates on the *dahara* (the small ether) and so forth as taught in the Śruti there is no dependence on time, the Smṛti declares that for practitioners of Yoga based on the Smṛti there is indeed dependence on time.

One might ask: why could the yogi not be the very same person who worships the "small" [space] and so forth as taught in the Smṛti? To this he says: "And that which is taught in the Smṛti. Action performed with the intention of propitiating the Lord is Yoga, according to the Smṛti: "He who performs the obligatory action without depending on the fruit of action—he is both a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) and a yogi."
The experience of non-agency preceded by *dhāraṇā* (steadfast concentration) is Sāṃkhya, according to the Smṛti: "Holding that 'the senses operate upon the objects of the senses'.
One might object: "Is it not improper for the Śruti and Smṛti to have different meanings, as this would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? Thus he raises the doubt: "But [as for] 'fire'..."
It was stated that there is a difference in meaning with respect to one who has taken up the [observance] at the [proper] time.
However, if the word "time" (kāla) refers to the deity by means of the recognition of the Vedic sense, then there is indeed identity of meaning; this is the purpose of the resolution.
Therefore, it is established that through the power of the knowledge (vidyā), the seeker who has gone to the highest state always attains the fruit. //21//
Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda.
Thus concludes the second quarter of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Departure and Movement."
The Third Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya.
By way of the path beginning with light, because that [attainment] is well-known [from scripture]. (BS 4.3.1)

Having thus determined the departure (utkrānti), he begins the [fourth] quarter (pāda) in order to determine the path to be traversed and the goal to be reached: "By the path beginning with light, because that is well-known.
Preceded by a restatement of what has occurred, he states the subject matter of the first section (adhikaraṇa)—the path—beginning with the words "As far as the world of Brahman" (āsṛti).
"Virajaḥ" means those who are free from passion, i.e., devoid of sin.
Doubt arises from conflicting scriptural statements.

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) holds that since it was previously stated that even one who has died at some time may attain the fruit, there is an option (vikalpa) that the departure occurs by whichever path is possible;
whereas the established conclusion (siddhānta) distinguishes that there is only one single path.
Due to the difference in modes of worship (*upāsanā*), there is a difference in the paths (*mārga*) to be meditated upon as subordinate to them, and this is also indicated by the word "only" (*eva*).

Furthermore, since there is a plurality of paths, it is logical that this particular path leads to the goal with speed; this would not be the case if there were only one single path—this is the meaning.

He establishes the final conclusion—that even though there is a difference in the modes of worship (*upāsanā*), there is no contradiction in the unity of the path, just as there is unity in the Brahman that is the object of worship—with the words "In this way" (*evam*).
The meaning of the reason is that this path is well-known.

He raises the objection regarding a difference in paths based on the scriptural statement of non-distinction—"And those who..."—arguing that this refers to those who possess knowledge of the path not previously mentioned: "It might be so."

The meaning of the resolution is that since it has been stated that there are many qualifiers such as "fire" and so forth for one and the same path, there is no difference in the path due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). He explains the unity of the destination with the words "For thus... (*tathā hi*).

"From afar," "long-lived," and "of Hiraṇyagarbha" refer to the fact that they dwell for many long years—that is, many *saṃvatsaras*—within the *kāryabrahman*. "Victory" (*jiti*) means victory everywhere;
"dawn" (*vyuṣṭi*) means pervasion; the meaning is that one attains that.

Thus, it has been stated that because the identity of the path is determined through recognition—just as there is an identity of the goal—the difference in context is irrelevant. Now, he explains the function of the particle *eva* ("only") and the word "speed" (*tvarā*), beginning with the words "As for that which... (*yattu*).

Because there is an absence of distinct rays at night, the word "only" (eva) is used to exclude the possibility that even a knower might fail to connect with the rays; it does not serve to exclude others.
The meaning is that just as there is delay on the worldly path, there is none on the path beginning with light (arcis), and thus the statement regarding speed is appropriate.
He states a supporting mark for the identity of the path with the words "Moreover" (api ca).

The sense is that if there were a multiplicity of auspicious paths, there would be no mention of a "third station. Even though the subsequent path is one, as in the case of the "path of light" (arcirādi), he says "many" [in the verse] to provide the reason for this qualification. //1//
Vāyu [is to be meditated upon] after the year, by means of both the general and the specific. 4.3.2.2.
Having stated that the unity of the path is presupposed, he explains the sequence of stages (parvakrama).

Having stated the purport of the section—that the relationship of qualifier and qualified is expressed in order, such that "from this [fire], this [wind] is next among those beginning with light"—he states the subject matter: "He reaches this...
Here, the subject matter is the wind, which is mentioned immediately after fire.

Regarding the doubt as to whether he [the soul] goes immediately after the fire consisting of light (*arcis*) or after the year (*saṃvatsara*), based on the textual sequence and the specific details to be mentioned later, the author begins with the established conclusion (siddhānta): "It is said. The meaning of the scripture is this:

the person—the worshiper—departs from this world, that is, from the body; for that person who has departed, that wind (*vāyu*) relaxes within itself—that is, it creates an opening—and through that door provided by the wind, which is like the hole in a chariot wheel, he goes upward to the sun. This is the meaning of the scriptural passage.
Now he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa): "Why again?
This means that by the force of the textual reading, air follows immediately after light;
this is merely the reading of the Kauṣītakins.
There is no word whatsoever that expresses a specific sequence;

however, for the Kāṇvas, because the sequence is determined by the two words "tena" (by that) and "ūrdhvam" (upwards), there is a sublation of the textual order—this is the meaning of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Let it be that in the path beginning with light as found in the Chāndogya, air follows after the year due to the mention of the year.

But since the word "year" (saṃvatsara) is not mentioned in the Vājin recension, how can it be said that "Vāyu is beyond the year"? To this he says: "The word 'vājī' [is used]. If that were so, the Sūtra would have been "from the world of the gods to Vāyu"; to this he says: "But [the Sūtra says] 'from the year to Vāyu'.

Since the year has months as its constituent parts, the sequence following the year is the month; beyond the year is the world of the gods, beyond that is Vāyu, and beyond Vāyu is Āditya. Thus the order is established in both scriptural texts.
The word "tena" (by that) indicates that, by virtue of the direct statement in the instrumental case, it is understood that Vāyu is preceded by Āditya;
however, it is established that in the Sūtra, the term "Vāyu" refers to the Vāyu who is preceded by the World of the Gods. //2//

Having thus stated the position of Vāyu, who is recited by the Kauṣītakins immediately after Agni, he now states the position of Varuṇa, who is recited immediately after Vāyu, within the path beginning with light (arcis): "Varuṇa is above lightning" because of their connection.

Regarding the doubt as to whether Varuṇa and the others, as recited [in the text], are connected as stages of the path or not, [the answer is given] by the ablative case in "from light, to day," etc., which indicates that light and the others [are stages].

Since Varuṇa and the others have no specific location mentioned for them—just as with the wind, which is bound by the sequence of the path and the mountains—they do not connect [with the stages] because they have not obtained a location; such being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the author states the established conclusion (siddhānta): "From the sun.
He provides the proof for the connection of the waters with lightning, stating: "It lightens."

The meaning is that, because Varuṇa is connected to lightning through the medium of water, and because of the maxim "that which is adventitious is placed at the end," Indra and Prajāpati follow immediately after lightning according to the order of the text. //3//
The [guides] are those who lead across, because of the indicative mark thereof. (BS 4.3.4)
Having thus determined the sequence of the light and the other stages, he now determines their essential nature: "They are conducting deities (ātivāhika), because of the indicative mark.
A doubt arises because of the similarity in the mention of signs and because of the word "world" (loka) as well as the indicative mark of being a leader.
The first two positions constitute the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).

He establishes the final conclusion—that the light and the others ending with lightning are conscious guides—by stating "Thus," etc., on the grounds that they are mentioned together with the superhuman person who acts as the guide.

An objection is raised with the words "That statement," suggesting that according to the literal text, the superhuman person alone should be the guide and not the light and the others. [The response is:

Since it would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda) if the passage were intended to convey both the superhuman nature and the guiding role of the person, the light and the others must be understood as the guides by virtue of the terms "light" and so forth.

Since human beings have been introduced [in the preceding passage], by the force of the context, a non-human (amānava) leader is obtained immediately after the lightning; therefore, it must be stated that by restating the leadership already established by the context, only the quality of being non-human is being taught. Thus he says: "No. The sense is that if the context concerning the leader were not accepted, the sentence "a non-human person leads" would be split, because leadership—just like the state of being non-human—would not have been previously established.
He takes up the sūtra which provides the supporting reasoning for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mention of leadership (*netṛtva*): "But surely... (nanv iti) //4//
Because that [cognition] is established through the confusion of both [subject and object], [it is not a valid means of knowledge]. (BBs 4.3.5)

If the light (*arci*) and the other stages were indeed non-intelligent and lacked a leader, then, due to the delusion and ignorance of both the path and its traveler, there would be no upward movement; therefore,

since it is established by the support of worldly logic that one who lacks self-effort must be led by another intelligent being, the aforementioned indicative mark (*liṅga*) is consistent with reason— this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
He refutes the two preceding positions with the words "because of instability," and so forth.

Since it has been stated that because the light, day, and other stages are unstable, there is no waiting for one who dies at night or other such times, they cannot be either markers of the path or objects of enjoyment;
however, if they are deities, the defect of instability does not apply—this is the meaning.
As for the claim that the status of being a sign appears from the natural force of the instruction itself, he says in response: "From light to day.
And because there is a doubt as to whether it is a sign or a guide, he states that the determination is made by means of the remainder of the passage: "Moreover."

Regarding what was stated—that there is the state of being an object of enjoyment (bhogyatva) from the word "world" (loka)—he says "no," beginning with the words "saṃpiṇḍita. He introduces another aphorism with the question: "How, moreover... //5//
Then, by means of the lightning alone, because of that scriptural statement; (BBs 4.3.6).
The meaning is that the non-human [being] comes from the world of lightning; thus, it is by means of the one belonging to lightning (vaidyuta).
In the Śruti, the meaning is "from the world of lightning.
The intention is that even though Varuṇa and the others do not act as direct leaders according to the Śruti, they are included within the path by virtue of being supportive. //6//
Bādari [holds that] this [self] has a task [to perform], because its going [to the world of Brahman] is logically possible. (BS 4.3.7)

Having thus ascertained the path, he considers the goal to be reached: "The effected [Brahman] (kārya) is this [goal], because going is possible for it"—this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Considering that, according to the prima facie view, the purpose of the path is liberation (*mukti*), whereas according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), its purpose is enjoyment (*bhoga*), he first states the established conclusion: "In that case, it is indeed the effected [Brahman].
Just as space, though all-pervading, can be a destination by virtue of being distinguished by another location, so too [the effected Brahman] is the goal to be reached.
It has been seen that, because Brahman is the innermost self (*pratyak*), it cannot be reached by any means whatsoever; this is the meaning. //7//
And because it has been specifically distinguished. (BBs 4.3.8)

He states that the supreme [Brahman] is not the destination because of the use of the plural number, the word "worlds" (*loka*), and the locative case indicating a locus, as well as because the place to be reached is distinguished from the Supreme. He says, "And because it is specified.

The meaning is that the scriptural mention of "worlds" with respect to the Supreme Brahman is figurative, based on the metaphorical application of the term "object of enjoyment" (*bhogya*) to the Supreme Brahman.

By the neuter word *brahman*, which denotes the cause, the effect is indicated in order to conform to the multiple scriptural passages characterized by the plural number and other features, which are supported by the logic of being a destination.
Furthermore, the Supreme is not the destination indicated by the mark of non-return;
for the meaning is that the mark is otherwise established through gradual liberation (kramamukti). //8//
"But that designation [of the Self] is due to proximity. (BS 4.3.9)
Because of the statement that [the soul] departs together with its presiding deity at the end of its task;
because of the traditional teaching (smṛti);
and because Jaimini holds that it goes to the highest [Brahman], since that is the primary sense.
The *pratisaṃcara* is the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

When that occurs, at the end of the supreme Hiraṇyagarbha—upon the cessation of the modifications consisting of the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-liṅga-śarīra*)—all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā who possess realized selves, pure intellects, and who have attained right knowledge there, are liberated along with Brahmā as he is being released. They [attain] the Supreme.
The construction is: "they enter the state" (*padaṃ praviśanti*).

Having thus stated the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) refuted by it, beginning with the words "But which [state]... (verse 9), verse 10, verse 11, and verse 12.
And because it is observed [in scripture]. (BBs 4.3.13)
In the Dahara-vidyā and in the Kaṭhavallīs, within the section concerning the Supreme Brahman, the departure [of the soul] is shown by the words, "Going upwards from there... (KaU 2.6.15). //13//
And there is no intention toward realization regarding the effect. (BBs 4.3.14)

Thus it has been stated that the journey concerns the Supreme Being (para) on account of the indications of Brahman and immortality, as well as from the context; now, however, he dispels the doubt that there is no goal beyond the Supreme—based on the scriptural statement regarding the meditator's resolve at the time of death to "attain the assembly hall and the palace of Prajāpati"—with the words: "Nor [to] the effected [Brahman]."
Because the subject under discussion is "another," and since the word *yaśas* (glory) is well-known as a name for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the Self is expressed by the word *yaśas*.
[The meaning is: "I become the glory, the Self, of the Brahmins."
Likewise, because of the indicative marks of universal identity—such as "the fame of kings" and "the fame of the Vaiśyas"—the meaning is that this is indeed the resolve for attaining the Supreme.

Or, let it be granted that the desire to reach the house has the Supreme Brahman as its object; nevertheless, how could that [desire] be preceded by a journey? To this, he says: "And that... [referring to the passage]:
"In that world of Brahman, there is an unconquered city built by the one who ordains knowledge, belonging to Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha. By him alone...
In the Dahara-vidyā, it is stated that "the wise man attains that golden mansion constructed and fashioned by the Lords," thus describing the attainment of the mansion as preceded by a journey.
Therefore, the meaning is that even in the case of the Supreme Brahman, its attainment is established as being preceded by a journey, due to the commonality of the term "attainment of a mansion."

Furthermore, since the root *pad* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with the meaning "to go," one might think that in the phrase "I enter the house" (*veśma prapadye*), there is an expectation of a path; thus he says, "even of *pad*" (*paderapi*).
He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
He then proceeds to conclude by reinforcing that the first [position] alone is the established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*), saying "those two" (*tāviti*).
He clarifies the fallacious nature of the reasons, such as the primary meaning of the word *brahman*, with the words "not indeed" (*na hi*).

The meaning is that because the state of being a destination, the use of the plural number in "in the worlds of Brahman" (*brahmalokeṣu*), and the scriptural statement regarding the attainment of divine enjoyments such as fragrance through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) are impossible in the case of the Supreme Brahman, one must abandon the primary sense [of the word].

Even though the word *brahman* occurs in such scriptural passages as "This, O Satyakāma, is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman," where its usage is common [to both], [the context here requires a different interpretation].

Although [the term "Brahman"] is primary in both senses due to its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), it should be understood that it is accepted as secondary with respect to the lower Brahman (*apara-brahman*) because, in the case of the Full Supreme [Brahman], the etymological meaning (*avayava-artha*)— namely, unsurpassed greatness— is obtained.
As it has been stated in the Kaṭhavallīs, by the force of the context, the "going" (*gati*) has the Supreme [Brahman] as its object.
To this he replies: "The other [knowledge]" (*pareti*).

Just as there is a mention of other channels not connected with it for the purpose of praising the Suṣumṇā which is connected with knowledge (*vidyā*), so too, even in the context of the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), there is a mention of the path based on lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) for the purpose of praising that [higher knowledge]. For even without the path, the higher knowledge possesses a result of unsurpassed excellence; however, within that [result], the fruit of the lower knowledge—which is accomplished by means of the path—is included. Thus, the meaning is that this is done to obtain praise.

As for what was said—that even the intention regarding attainment refers to the subject under discussion, namely the Supreme (Brahman)—he says "no," citing the passage beginning with "of Prajāpati. For the context is set by the scriptural references to the hall of Prajāpati and his abode, as well as by the statement that he is composed of those [elements]. This context overrides [the previous argument].
The meaning is that the identification with all things (*sārvātmya*) expressed as "I am glory" is employed for the purpose of meditation upon the lower Brahman.
Having stated his own position, he refutes the opposing view with the words "some say," etc.

[He argues that] even though Brahman is omnipresent and constitutes one's very self, it might still be something to be reached by moving from one place to another different from the location of *saṃsāra*, or from one time to another different from that time; this is shown through the two examples of the earth and age.
He raises an objection with "nanu":
non-difference is already established even without effort, because of the non-distinction between a state and that which possesses the state, [the latter] being identical with its own self.

Now, one might object: it is indeed logical that the earth and age, even though already attained, can still be objects of going because they are qualified by different locations and times, and because they are distinct from the goer;
but how can Brahman, which is non-different from the goer, be an object of going? To this he replies: "possessing all powers" (*sarvaśakti*).

That earth which has been attained cannot be an object of going, and as for that other location which is to be gone to, it is not actually attained [as such]. How, then, can there be a state of being an object of going for what is already attained? As for age, too, it is merely a manifestation at another time.
The reality of things is that there is no "state of being an object to be gone to.

Having provisionally accepted that the earth and time are objects to be gone to, [the author] states with the words beginning "no" (*na*) that the Supreme Brahman cannot be an object to be gone to in any way whatsoever, because it lacks the distinctions of space and time.

The scriptural tradition (smṛti) beginning with "The supreme Brahman is without beginning" [supports this], and the logical principle (*nyāya*) is that the Self, which is pure vision, is devoid of attributes because the specific objects of vision are merely imagined within that vision.

One might raise the objection that Brahman with attributes alone—specifically as the *sūtrātman*—is the supreme goal to be reached, and that Brahman devoid of distinctions does not exist at all; this is expressed in the phrase "jagadutpatti" (regarding the origin of the world).

Is the non-existence of the attributeless [Brahman] due to the absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), or due to contradiction with the scriptures (*śruti*) concerning [Brahman] with attributes?
"No," he says, [denying] "not so.
He raises the second objection: "origination and so forth.

He replies, "No," stating that there is no contradiction because the scriptural passages concerning the qualified [Brahman] are supplementary to the scriptural passages concerning the unqualified [Brahman].

He asks "Why? [in response to the question]: why should it not be the case that the scriptures concerning the featureless (nirviśeṣa) are themselves supplementary to the scriptures concerning the qualified (saviśeṣa)?

He replies with the words beginning "It is said" (ucyate), stating that because those [scriptures on the featureless] are complete in themselves due to their fruitfulness regarding their own subject matter, they have no further expectancy; whereas the qualified scriptures, being fruitless in themselves, serve as supplements by way of providing the specific objects to be negated, according to the maxim: "That which is fruitless in the proximity of that which is fruitful is a subordinate part of the latter."
He states that "it is not only by logic (nyāya) that [Brahman] is the remainder, but also by direct scriptural statement (śruti)" with the words "But it is directly perceived" (pratyakṣaṃ tu).

In that regard, having begun in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad with the statement, "From that root-cause, Brahman, this sprout consisting of the world as its effect has arisen," and concluding with, "By means of that sprout, seek out its root," the fact that Being alone is the object to be known is declared.

Likewise, even in the Taittirīyaka, by restating the origination of the world and so forth, it is shown that Brahman alone is the object of knowledge; therefore, the meaning is that the scriptural texts concerning creation are shown by scripture itself to be subordinate to the cognition of the undifferentiated [Brahman].
Having thus established that because Brahman is devoid of attributes there is no "going" [to it], he states the conclusion: "Thus...
Furthermore, because there is an explicit negation, he states that the Supreme is not a destination: "Not of Him..."

Having thus rejected the [notion of] motion by means of the analysis of the path to be traversed (*gantavya*), he rejects it by means of the analysis of the goer (*gantr*) as well, starting with the words "And in the conceptualization of motion," and so forth.
There are two conceptualizations based on difference and non-difference; the third conceptualization is absolute difference (*atyantabheda*).
Now, why is the conceptualization of absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*) not mentioned?
Regarding this, he says "absolutely" (*atyantam*). He asks what the fault is in the three alternatives with the words "if it were so" (*yady evam*).
He states another defect in both of the two remaining alternatives with the words "in the cases of modification and part" (*vikārāvayavapakṣayoś ca*).
Since Brahman, as qualified by the individual soul (*jīva*) which is of the nature of a modification and a part [of that Brahman], is eternal, there could be no going and coming for souls;
for there is no movement in the two parts of a frog and a stone that reside within an immovable, massive rock—this is the sense.
However, according to our view, the delusion of going and coming arises from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) imagined through ignorance (*ajñāna*); this is the underlying intention.
Having restated the third alternative and having analyzed it, he refutes it with the words beginning "Now" (*atha*).

The proponent of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*) says—referring to the phrase "of the modification and the part"—that "I have no fault in the form of contradiction with the scriptural texts on non-difference.
He [the author] replies, "No," because a primary non-difference between two things that are distinct is not logical due to their mutual opposition.

Furthermore, all three positions are untenable; for if the state of being a transmigrator—which is the transmigrator’s real status as a living soul (jīva)—were destroyed, it would follow that the real nature of the living soul itself is destroyed.

Nor have you, like us, accepted that the identity with Brahman is the living soul’s real form such that it would not perish even when its transmigratory state perishes; thus he says, "In all... [sarveṣu].
But what is the use of this identity with Brahman?

Having set forth the view of those dull-witted by nature—that liberation (mokṣa) is indeed the non-existence of saṃsāra, and that this will be accomplished merely through the absence of karma—he refutes it with the words beginning "yattu" (but as for that).
"That" means:
because there is a lack of valid evidence (pramāṇa) for the claim that such conduct is the cause of liberation.
To the objection that reasoning alone is the means of knowledge, he says: "And this cannot even be reasoned. Now, one might object:

"Even for you, this is merely a matter of reasoning, since it is impossible to experience in a single birth the fruits of various contradictory karmas; therefore, there must remain residual karma which serves as the cause for another birth. Anticipating this doubt, he states the proof for that [residual karma]: "And the establishment of the existence of residual karma."

He raises the objection that there might be no further birth because accumulated merit and demerit whose fruits have not yet begun are exhausted through the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) and so forth—this is expressed by the words "It might be thus.

However, merit does not destroy merit because they are not mutually contradictory; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle. Furthermore, there is no proof that demerit is entirely destroyed by merit. Therefore, he states with the words "That is not so" (*tan na*) and following, that a future birth resulting from accumulated merit and demerit is unavoidable.

He says "nor by the obligatory [rites]" (na ca nitya) because birth could also result from the performance of obligatory rites and so forth, given the non-specific scriptural statement, "By action, the world of the ancestors," as well as the Smṛti.

When one's regular conduct, such as obligatory rites (*nitya*), is performed for the purpose of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), another result subsequently arises; regarding this, there is an illustration:
"Just as" (*tadyathā*) means when something has been fashioned or superimposed.
Nevertheless, since there is no certainty regarding the existence of karma such as that performed for specific desires (kāmyakarma), he says: "But it must be doubted.
The implication is that in your position, there is a flaw because one cannot attain the certainty that liberation occurs at the fall of the body solely through knowledge.
Furthermore, he says "nor" to show that even the hope for liberation is not tenable for a soul (jīva) distinct from Brahman, whose inherent nature consists of agency and so forth.

One might object: "The effect, such as agency and so forth, is not the [inherent] nature [of the Self], but rather its power (śakti). To this, [the author] replies: "It might be so. Since a power that is known through its effects cannot logically exist if the effect is never produced, if that power were to exist, then—because it would be eternally connected to its object (the effect) and to the causes such as unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), place, time, and so forth, by way of the Self and the power itself—liberation (mokṣa) would be impossible.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "And that," etc.

Having raised the doubt as to how transmigratory existence could be possible if the individual soul (jīva) is admitted to be Brahman for the sake of establishing liberation, he recalls what has been stated more than once—that its possibility arises from ignorance—with the words "From the Supreme," etc.
Having resolved this incidental matter, he concludes the primary subject at hand with the words "Thus, therefore."

[Objection: But is it not the case that even in the context of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), movement is heard [in scripture] by means of the word "attains"? To this he says: "The knower of Brahman attains... [He further states] "Moreover... because movement is fruitless, it does not have the higher [Brahman] as its object.
He refutes the position that it refers to meditative reflection (*anucintana*) by saying: "And not [to that which is] eternally established."

Anticipating the objection as to how some have stated that the movement [of the soul] has another realm as its object, he says "there, the higher and lower... to indicate that such a view is erroneous.
By first posing the question "Are there two? and so forth, he explains the division between the higher and lower Brahman, stating that the movement is purposeful with respect to the lower Brahman.
To the question of how there can be movement for a soul that is all-pervading, he replies: "Even though it is omnipresent... (14).
"Bādarāyaṇa maintains that [the Lord] leads those who have not taken hold of the symbols, because there would be faults in both cases, and because of the nature of their resolve" (BBs 4.3.15).
Having thus determined the manner of going, he identifies those who go with the words "not by symbols" (*apratīka*).
This is because of the general scriptural statement, "He alone leads them to Brahman," and because of the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).
He states the doubt with the word "this" (*idam*).

In the section concerning non-restriction (*aniyamādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that for all worshippers other than the knower of reality (*tattvavit*), there is the inclusion [of the path] of the way [to the world of Brahmā]. Now, if it were stated that the path belongs only to those who worship the non-manifest (*apratīka*) and not to all worshippers of the modifications (*vikāra*), there would be a contradiction with what was previously stated.
Therefore, the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the attainment of the higher path is established for every worshipper whatsoever.
In the established doctrine (siddhānta), however, there is the establishment of both states;
the phrase "because it is not a fault" (*adoṣāt*) in the Sūtra is a separate section, meaning "because there is no contradiction" (*avirodhāt*).
The intention [of the author] is that in the sūtra "There is no restriction for all," the word "all" excludes those who meditate on symbols (pratīka).

Although it must be said that for those who meditate on symbols the path beginning with light (arcirādi) applies—since they do not enter either the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) or the third station—nevertheless, let their journey extend only as far as lightning; there is no attainment of Brahman, because they lack the "intentionality toward Brahman" (brahmakratutva).
For the principle of "according to one's intention" (tatkratu-nyāya)—that "whatever one meditates upon, that one attains"—is rooted in scripture.
Furthermore, since names and so forth—which are the objects of meditation (*dhyeya*)—are merely attributes (*guṇa*) of Brahman, there is no meditating upon Brahman itself [in those cases].

The meaning of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya is that this general principle is set aside by an explicit statement (*āhatyavāda*), that is, by a direct scriptural declaration, as seen in the case of the "Knowledge of the Five Fires" (*pañcāgnividyā*). //15//
And it demonstrates a distinction. BBs_4,3.16.
Furthermore, because scripture teaches a gradation of fruits according to the gradation of symbols, those who meditate on symbols do not attain Brahman; thus he says, "And [there is] a distinction.
Therefore, in the absence of a specific scriptural statement to the contrary, it is established that only those who meditate on Brahman go to Brahman. //16//
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Govindānanda Bhagavat. //3//
Thus ends the third quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Northern Path for One Who Possesses Knowledge with Attributes and Has Died.
"Manifestation upon attaining [Brahman], by its own nature, on account of the scriptural statement.
(BBs 4.4.1) In the preceding section, the attainment of the effected Brahman (*kāryabrahma*) by those who meditate upon Brahman was described.

Now, intending to elaborate in the latter half of this section upon their specific lordly powers (*aiśvarya*) pertaining to the world of Brahman (*brāhmalaukika*), the author first states the state of being the undifferentiated Brahman—which is attained through the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) that is most venerable—beginning with: "Manifestation upon attaining..."
Because of the word "own" (*sva*).

Considering that the logical principle (*nyāya*) is contradicted by the hearing of its own word (*svaśabda*), and that "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*) refers to the function of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), while the arising of the destruction of bondage is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), he establishes the final conclusion with the words "Thus" (*evam*). The meaning is as follows: it is appropriate that the word "own" (*sva*) is intended to exclude the idea that liberation, as a fruit, is something newly acquired or adventitious; however, if it were to mean "one's own," it would be a redundant restatement of what is already established. //1//
He cites another sūtra: "What more?

For in the waking state, one possesses bodily attributes such as blindness; however, in a dream, one is actually killed by someone, and moreover, one even seems to weep due to the loss of a son or other loved ones.
But in deep sleep, because of the absence of specific cognition, [the self] is as if destroyed;

whereas in the state of bondage it remains with a defiled nature, in liberation, however, it abides as the self of full bliss, shining forth on all sides with all suffering dissolved— this is the meaning of the great distinction.
