Because it is seen as non-different.

Since there is doubt regarding the difference or non-difference of Brahman due to the disputes of various proponents concerning liberation—which is said to consist in abiding in one's own nature—he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of absolute difference and then declares the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "Of whom... (yasya). //4//
Jaimini [holds that the soul is] of the nature of Brahman, on account of the introductory statement and other [indications]. (BS 4.4.5)

Jaimini has stated that regarding the nature of Brahman as taught by Bādarāyaṇa, there is a disagreement among sages: does He abide endowed with real attributes such as omniscience and the like; or, because those attributes are absolutely non-existent—like the horn of a hare—does He abide as pure consciousness alone; or, while being in reality pure consciousness, does He possess imagined omniscience and so forth from the perspective of the empirical dealings of other individual souls? This constitutes the divergence of opinion among the sages.
Since there is doubt, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) first with the words "now," and so forth.
It should be understood that the very establishment of each respective position is the result.

The meaning of the injunction "he is to be sought" is the subject of reference (*uddeśa*), while the formulation beginning with "that which is the Self" (*ya ātmā*) constitutes the meaning of the explanatory statement (*upanyāsa*).
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādipadāt*), the mention of "injunction" (*vidhi*) is included.
Among these, an injunction is that which makes known what was previously unknown; he states this with the words "so [he is] there.

However, the designation "omniscient" and so forth is indeed not a mere reference (*uddeśa*); because there is no injunction, it is not an injunction either, since it is stated as an established fact—this is the meaning. //5//
"By means of consciousness alone [the soul departs], because it consists of that," so says Auḍulomi (BBs 4.4.6).
Refuting the reality of properties such as "truth" (satyatva) and so forth, he states the position of their absolute non-existence with the words "by mere consciousness" (cititanmātreṇa).
"Consciousness" (citi) means sentience (caitanya);

those [properties] which arise from conceptual constructions (vikalpa)—such as verbal knowledge and the like—which are unreal cognitions, are "absolutely non-existent" (atyantāsanta), that is to say, they do not exist at all.

Anticipating the objection that while non-existent entities (abhāva-dharma) may lack existence, existent entities (bhāva-dharma) must possess it, he states "satyakāma" etc., asserting that even these lack existence because they are merely adventitious (aupādhika). To the question of how scriptural passages concerning eating and so forth apply to the liberated one who is pure consciousness (cinmātra), he says "ata eva ca":
the meaning is precisely because of the negation of all attributes (dharma). //6//
Even so, because of the introductory statement and because [the soul] exists previously, Bādarāyaṇa maintains that there is no contradiction. (BS 4.4.7)

The two positions—that phenomena are real or that they are absolutely non-existent—are untenable; for this would result in the subversion of the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*) as well as the scriptural texts and conventional usage regarding omniscience and other attributes. Therefore, he establishes the third position as superior with the words "even so" (*evamapi*).

Here, some are deluded, thinking: "Since liberation arises from the knowledge of undivided pure consciousness (*akhaṇḍacinmātra*), there is an absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*); how then can there be a connection with phenomena born of ignorance?"
They should be instructed as follows:
those very attributes of Īśvara are designated by other liberated souls within the conscious self (cidātman).
Nor should it be argued that because there is only one primordial ignorance (mūlāvidyā), once it is destroyed, how could there be another liberated soul?
We do not say that upon its destruction there is the activity of another soul;

rather, we say that when a portion [of the primal ignorance] is destroyed, those souls who were previously characterized by the conceit of possessing the two internal bodies (ādhibhautika and ādhyātmika) composed of that portion become liberated, while other souls—conditioned by different limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—act as agents.
If it is asked: "In that case, why is the position of manifold ignorance (anekavidyāpakṣa) not accepted, since the plurality of souls is necessary? We reply: No.

The view that there is a plurality of primordial natures (*prakṛti*) and a differentiation of the phenomenal world for each individual soul is rejected because it involves the unwarranted assumption of numerous entities. Therefore, the position of a single ignorance (*ekāvidyā*), which is accepted by all the elders, is superior;
and the distinction between bondage and liberation is established through the differentiation of parts—this is the summary. //7//
But [the creation of the world occurs] from mere volition alone, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (BS 4.4.8)

Thus, the fruit of higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) has been stated; now, the fruit of lower knowledge (*aparavidyā*) is elaborated: "But [it is] from mere volition alone, because of the scriptural statement.

Since the particle "alone" (*eva*) is common to both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with something else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), there arises a doubt:
does the volition of the worshiper who has gone to the world of Brahman depend upon another effort?

The meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: [The fulfillment of desires arises] because it is a conceptualization of the totality of enjoyments, just like the conceptualization of ourselves and others. Nor is there any contradiction with the particle *eva* (only), because by means of the conceptualization, it excludes the impossibility of the totality [of conditions], thereby signifying ease; for if effort were not admitted, the nourishment of enjoyment would not be established.
In this context, the result is the conformity with worldly conduct;
however, the Veda teaches that in the established doctrine (siddhānta), by the power of knowledge (vidyā), it is the mere volition itself that brings about the fulfillment of enjoyment.

Furthermore, if even after the volition for enjoyment there were a dependence upon other causes to be accomplished through further effort, then [the result would depend] upon the attainment of those causes.

Since there would otherwise be a failure of a previously formed resolve due to delay in the enjoyment [of its fruit], the scripture stating that his resolves are true (*satya-saṃkalpa*) implies that no other effort is required; thus he says: "But even another cause... (Sūtra 4.4.8).
And for this very reason, he has no other lord. 4.4.9.
Now, one might ask: how can the accomplishment of enjoyment through mere volition occur for the knower who is dependent on the Lord? To this he says: "For this very reason.
The sense is that since the attributes of the Lord themselves have become manifest in the knower, there is no failure of his volition. //9//
Bādari maintains that there is non-existence [of the soul after death], for it is so stated [in scripture]. (BS 4.4.10)
"Jaimini [maintains] existence, because of the mention of mental volition (vikalpāmanana).

By the qualification "with the mind alone," which—like the word "only"—excludes connection with anything else, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) argues for non-existence, [claiming] there is an absence of body and so forth; thus Bādari says "non-existence," for it is so stated [in scripture].
Here too, doubt arises due to the disagreement among disputants.
In this regard, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) consists of two alternatives: that the body and so forth do not exist at all, or that they always exist.
The established conclusion (*siddhāntapakṣa*) should be understood as the view that they exist or do not exist according to one's will and depending on the difference in time.
The distinction is that the result is the preeminence of the respective scriptural texts. // 10 // // 11 //

"Like the twelve-day sacrifice":

since the twelve-day sacrifice is understood from the scriptural injunction of "entering" (upāyi), as in "those who, knowing thus, enter the sacrificial session (satra)," its status as a *satra* is established;
for the definition of a *satra* is that it is enjoined either by the term "they sit" (*āsate*) or by the term "they enter" (*upayanti*). This is the settled conclusion.

Likewise, because the injunction "one should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite" (dvādaśāhena prajākāmaṃ yājayet) is seen as a *yajati*-codanā (a prescription for a sacrifice), its status as an *ahīna* (non-soma-less sacrifice) is understood through the realization that it has a fixed performer, just like the *dvirātra* and other such rites; this is the meaning. // 12 // // 13 // // 14 //
The entry [of the individual soul] is like that of a lamp; for thus scripture shows. (BS 4.4.15)
The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp.
Because one observes both [states]—[the soul's presence] through mere volition and its inhabiting of created bodies—the author states a doubt with the word "existence" (bhāvam).

The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) concludes that since the beginningless subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) exists in only a single physical body, the experience of enjoyment in multiple created bodies is impossible.
Considering that this is established in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), he explains the Sūtra with the words "Just as... and so forth.
By such scriptural passages as "He becomes one-fold, three-fold, five-fold," etc., it is stated that the transformation into manifold forms belongs only to the knower (*vidvān*).
However, the knower is neither the body nor pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
However, the self is conditioned by the subtle body (liṅga),
and its multiplicity is not possible without a difference in those subtle bodies.
Therefore, on the strength of scripture, one must accept that this single, beginningless subtle body undergoes differentiation by entering into multiple bodies.

Although there is an absolute difference between the original lamp and the lamps produced in other wicks, there is no difference in the subtle body (*liṅga*) caused by a difference in the body; for the difference is not intrinsic.
If the subtle body were different in itself, then because the individual souls (*jīva*) conditioned by them would also be different, the impossibility of recollection (*anusaṃdhāna*) would follow.
Furthermore, the creation of multiple adventitious subtle bodies would result in the fallacy of the theory that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*).

Nevertheless, because the unity of individual instances is superimposed upon them through the identity of the universal "lamp-ness," the similarity between the illustration and the illustrated must be understood.

Thus, just as a lamp enters into many wicks, so too, by the power of yoga and knowledge, the knower simultaneously enters into multiple bodies due to the pervasiveness of the knower's subtle body (*liṅga*); this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
He says, "This is not so," because the fact that the knower possesses multiple states is heard in scripture and would otherwise be untenable.
For this reason as well, he states that [the mind] possesses a self (*sātmakatva*): "And not of those that are soulless" (*na ca nirātmakānām*).
That beginningless mind which resides in one body, the minds residing in other bodies follow its lead; for it is possible for those [minds] existing in those [other bodies] to be governed by it.
Regarding this, he cites the consensus of the Yogaśāstra: "This very... (*eṣaiva*).
"From mere *asmitā* (the sense of 'I-am-ness'), the minds of emanation proceed; a single mind is the motivator for many"—thus was it aphorized by the Blessed Patañjali.

This is according to the Vedic revelation: "May he impel our intellects.

Indicating the completion of the treatise, he honors the author of the Sūtras with the word "Bhagavān.
His status as Bhagavān consists in his omniscience;
his status as Ācārya (Teacher) arises from establishing his disciples in right conduct by means of the Sūtras.

By the use of the term "Bādarāyaṇa," which indicates residence at Badarikāśrama, [the author] manifests the grace of Nārāyaṇa, the eternal omniscient Supreme Teacher; thereby, he demonstrates the faultlessness of the scripture composed by him. Although knowledge of the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman yields a result that is subject to degrees of excellence, from that [knowledge], there is no return [to saṃsāra] through the knowledge of the unqualified (nirguṇa); thus he says: "No return, on account of the scriptural statement; no return, on account of the scriptural statement. The connection is as follows: those who go to the world of Brahman, having reached it, do not return.
He specifies the world by the words "in which":

in that Brahma-world which is in the third heaven from here, from this earthly world; there, the two syllables *ara* and *ṇya* are equal to the nectar-heart (*sudhā-hṛda*), meaning they consist of food (*anna-maya*). *Aira* means consisting of food.
"My lake is intoxicating; it is Soma-savana, raining nectar.

Although there is no returning for them here to this human world according to the Śrutis, because of the qualification "to this" (*imam*), it appears that those who have gone to the world of Brahmā in this *kalpa* return in another *kalpa*.

Nevertheless, for those who have gone [to the world of Brahman] by means of practices such as the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and firm celibacy (*brahmacarya*) without the worship of the Lord (*īśvara*), there would be a return due to the absence of the necessity of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

However, for those who have gone by means of the worship of the Lord in the "small [space]" (*dahara*) and so forth, liberation occurs through the knowledge of the Self obtained by the unimpeded grace of the Lord, even when the fruit of that qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*) has exhausted; having this in mind, he says: "But even though there is finitude... (*antavattve 'pi tu...*) .

Now, one might raise the objection: "In this context, the author of the Sūtras has stated the sequence of non-return only for those who know the Saguna Brahman, not for those who know the Nirguna; what is the reason for that? Anticipating this, he says "samyak" (perfectly), meaning "by taking recourse to that.
This implies that while the possibility of return might arise for those who know the Saguna, non-return is established precisely by taking recourse to perfect realization (*samyagdarśana*).
Therefore, the meaning is: what need is there to say that for those who possess right vision (*samyagdarśin*), there is no possibility of returning?
Wherever a chapter concludes, the repetition of only a single word has been shown;

here, however, because of the repetition of the entire *sūtra* itself, the conclusion of the treatise is indicated. Thus he says: "No return, on account of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*).

Thus, by means of the statement on systematic concordance (*samanvaya*), it has been determined that the identity of Brahman and the Self is established by the authority of the Vedānta; all contradictions regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences—such as those arising from memory or logic—have been removed, and the perfection of the means [of knowledge] has been demonstrated.

Therefore, for one who possesses the means such as discrimination and whose entire obstructions have been dispelled through repeated hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, there occurs the destruction of bondage along with its root through the realization of the indivisible Self.
Thus it is established that [liberation] consists in abiding as the Self, which is truth, stainless, infinite, self-luminous consciousness-bliss. //22//
Having thoroughly examined various collections of texts according to my own understanding,
this commentary on the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* has been composed for the delight of the virtuous. (1)

The Inner Controller, the witness of the universe, the creator of all, and the scion of Raghu—therefore, no fault can be suspected here, for according to the teaching, "He alone indeed [is the agent]. (2)

Having beheld upon the chest, the eyes, the sides, and the pair of palms of Rāma— [the Lord] who possesses the luster of the Kaustubha gem, compassion, Sītā, the initiation of the bow, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons— the commentary named *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, having fixed its mind in its heart as to where it might find union with the body of Rāma,
and being solely intent on attaining the bliss of its own Self, has sought refuge at the pair of lotus feet of the best of the Raghus. (3)

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā*, a commentary on the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* (Brahma-sūtra), composed by the venerable Govindānanda Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Gopālasarasvatī, the worshipful teacher among the illustrious Paramahaṃsa wandering mendicants.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Brahman and Abiding in the World of Brahman."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Fruit," in the venerable Śaṅkara-bhāṣya on the Brahma-sūtras.
Oṃ tat sat.
